title: Mental Health and Psychiatric Nursing
description: Concepts of mental health, the mental state examination, major psychiatric disorders, therapeutic relationships, psychotropic drug care, and mental health law and services in Nigeria.

topics.title: Concepts of Mental Health and Illness
topics.summary: Definitions, causes, stigma, and mental health services and law in Nigeria.

notes.b: WHO defines mental health as a state of well-being in which a person realises their abilities, can cope with normal stresses, work productively and contribute to the community. Mental disorders result from interacting biological (genetics, neurotransmitters, brain injury, substance use), psychological (trauma, personality, coping) and social factors (poverty, unemployment, conflict, displacement, family problems) — the biopsychosocial model. In Nigeria, mental illness is common but heavily stigmatised; many people first consult religious or traditional healers, where patients may be chained or maltreated. Services are concentrated in federal neuropsychiatric hospitals (e.g. Yaba, Aro in Abeokuta — site of pioneering community psychiatry by Thomas Adeoye Lambo) and teaching hospitals, with few psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses per population.
k: Stigma; first contact often faith/traditional healers

notes.b: The Lunacy Act of 1958 was long criticised for stigmatising language and inadequate rights protection; the National Mental Health Act 2021 repealed it, promoting human rights, community-based care, voluntary treatment where possible, safeguards for involuntary admission, and integration of mental health into primary care. The WHO mhGAP (Mental Health Gap Action Programme) trains non-specialist health workers to manage priority conditions (depression, psychosis, epilepsy, child disorders, dementia, substance use, self-harm). Nurses advocate for patients' rights, dignity and least-restrictive care, and combat stigma through education.
k: National Mental Health Act 2021 repealed the Lunacy Act 1958

topics.title: Assessment: History and Mental State Examination
topics.summary: Psychiatric history, the mental state examination, risk assessment and common signs.

notes.b: The mental state examination (MSE) describes the patient's current mental functioning: Appearance and behaviour (grooming, eye contact, psychomotor activity); Speech (rate, volume, tone, flow — pressured speech in mania, poverty of speech in depression or schizophrenia); Mood (patient's description) and affect (observed emotion — flat, blunted, labile, incongruent); Thought form (flight of ideas, loosening of associations, thought block) and content (delusions, obsessions, suicidal and homicidal thoughts); Perception (hallucinations — perceptions without a stimulus, most commonly auditory in schizophrenia; illusions — misperceptions of real stimuli); Cognition (orientation, attention, memory — e.g. Mini-Mental State Examination); and Insight and judgement.
k: MSE: appearance, speech, mood/affect, thought, perception, cognition, insight
Illusion: misperception of a real stimulus

notes.b: Every psychiatric assessment includes risk to self (suicide and self-harm, self-neglect), risk to others (violence) and risk from others (exploitation, abuse). Suicide risk factors: previous attempts (strongest predictor), depression, psychosis, substance misuse, hopelessness, recent loss, chronic illness, social isolation, male sex, access to means (pesticides, firearms) and a clear plan. Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk. Management of high risk: supervision (close observation), remove means, involve family, urgent specialist care. Collateral history from relatives is often essential.
k: Assess risk to self, others and from others
Asking about suicide does not increase risk

topics.title: Psychotic and Mood Disorders
topics.summary: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression and their nursing management.

notes.b: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder with positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations — often third-person auditory, thought disorder, disorganised behaviour), negative symptoms (blunted affect, alogia, avolition, social withdrawal) and cognitive impairment, usually beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood. Cannabis use increases risk. Treatment: antipsychotics (oral or long-acting depot injections to improve adherence), psychoeducation, family support, psychosocial rehabilitation and relapse prevention. Nursing care includes building trust, not arguing about delusions but not reinforcing them, ensuring safety, monitoring side effects (extrapyramidal symptoms, metabolic effects, neuroleptic malignant syndrome), promoting adherence and self-care.
k: Don't argue about or reinforce delusions

notes.b: Major depressive disorder: persistent low mood and/or loss of interest (anhedonia) for at least two weeks with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, guilt, psychomotor change and suicidal thoughts; in Nigeria depression often presents with somatic complaints (e.g. headache, 'heat in the head', body pains). Treatment: psychological therapies (CBT, problem-solving), antidepressants (SSRIs such as fluoxetine), and ECT for severe or psychotic depression. Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania (elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, risky behaviour) and depression; mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate, carbamazepine) and antipsychotics are used. Nursing care in mania: calm, low-stimulus environment, consistent limits, nutrition and hydration, sleep, safety.
k: SSRIs, CBT; ECT for severe cases

topics.title: Anxiety, Substance Use and Other Disorders
topics.summary: Anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, dementia and delirium, and child mental health.

notes.b: Anxiety disorders include generalised anxiety disorder (excessive worry most days for months), panic disorder (recurrent sudden panic attacks with palpitations, breathlessness, fear of dying), phobias, obsessive–compulsive disorder (intrusive thoughts and repetitive rituals) and post-traumatic stress disorder (re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal after trauma — common after insurgency, kidnapping and violence). Treatment: psychological therapies (CBT, exposure), SSRIs; benzodiazepines only short-term. Substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, tramadol, codeine syrup, methamphetamine) involve craving, loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal and continued use despite harm. Management: screening (e.g. CAGE for alcohol), brief interventions, detoxification (benzodiazepines and thiamine for alcohol withdrawal), rehabilitation, relapse prevention and harm reduction.
k: CBT and SSRIs; benzodiazepines short-term only
PTSD common after violence and kidnapping
CAGE screening; thiamine in alcohol withdrawal

notes.b: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by a physical illness (infection, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance, drugs, alcohol withdrawal) — a medical emergency; treat the cause, reorient the patient, ensure a calm, well-lit environment and involve family. Dementia is a chronic, progressive decline in memory and other cognitive functions (Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia); care focuses on safety, routine, support for carers and dignity. Childhood disorders include attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, conduct disorders and epilepsy-related problems; early identification, family support and education are key. Epilepsy is often managed within mental health services in Nigeria and carries significant stigma.

topics.title: Therapeutic Relationship and Interventions
topics.summary: Nurse–patient relationship, communication, de-escalation, psychotherapies and ECT care.

notes.b: The therapeutic nurse–patient relationship (Peplau) progresses through orientation, working (identification and exploitation) and termination phases. Key skills: active listening, empathy, genuineness, unconditional positive regard (Carl Rogers), open questions, reflection, silence, and maintaining professional boundaries. De-escalation of aggression: approach calmly, maintain a safe distance and exit route, speak softly, listen, acknowledge feelings, offer choices, avoid threatening postures; physical restraint and rapid tranquillisation are last resorts, used for the shortest time with monitoring and documentation. Seclusion and restraint must follow legal and institutional policies.

Psychological interventions include cognitive behavioural therapy (identifying and changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviours), problem-solving therapy, interpersonal therapy, family therapy, group therapy and psychoeducation; task-shifted interventions such as the Friendship Bench and WHO's Problem Management Plus are delivered by lay health workers. Occupational and recreational therapy promote rehabilitation. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is effective for severe or psychotic depression, catatonia and treatment-resistant conditions; nursing care before ECT includes consent, fasting, removing dentures and jewellery, and baseline observations; after ECT, monitor vital signs, orientation and airway, and reassure about transient memory loss and headache.
k: ECT for severe depression and catatonia
